title: Robert Eggers Wants a Break From Horror After Werwulf
excerpt:
The Nosferatu filmmaker says he is eager to explore work beyond horror.
His next planned project is an adaptation of Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet.
body_md:
Robert Eggers has become closely associated with meticulously researched, visually distinctive stories of dread, but he is ready to explore another direction. Speaking during a question-and-answer session in Mexico, the filmmaker said he does not want his career to become an endless sequence of signature horror productions. His comments suggest a temporary change in creative focus rather than a permanent departure from the genre.

His upcoming film Werwulf is scheduled for Christmas Day, December 25, 2026. Set in fourteenth-century England, the story follows a community threatened by a terrifying beast and a man whose family is endangered by its presence. Aaron Taylor-Johnson leads the cast, alongside Lily-Rose Depp and Willem Dafoe. The historical setting and supernatural threat place the project firmly within the territory audiences associate with Eggers.

That association has been built across several very different films. The Witch, released in 2015, explored religious fear and accusations of witchcraft. The Lighthouse, from 2019, transformed isolation and maritime folklore into psychological turmoil. Nosferatu, released in 2024, offered his interpretation of the vampire legend. Each film combined period detail with an intensely personal filmmaking approach.

Eggers also addressed the much-debated label elevated horror. He argued that serious horror films concerned with human darkness existed long before the term became fashionable. He cited the 2014 film It Follows as an important point in the contemporary discussion while acknowledging that Ti West had pursued similar work earlier.

In his view, many filmmakers with individual voices have discovered that genre cinema can provide a practical route to financing personal stories. That does not mean commercially oriented horror is without artistic merit. Eggers specifically recognized the success and effectiveness of James Wan's Insidious and The Conjuring films while discussing the broad appetite for horror over the past decade.

His next planned change of direction is an adaptation of William Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet for Focus Features. The project is hardly an escape from darkness in the conventional sense: the play is a tragedy shaped by family conflict, youthful love and death. Eggers previously joked that, after developing another especially bleak horror screenplay, he decided he needed a break and turned toward a story about two teenagers who die.

The contrast may ultimately be less about abandoning unsettling subject matter than about changing the dramatic framework through which he explores it. His careful attention to language, setting and historical atmosphere could prove well suited to Shakespeare, although specific production details and a release date have not yet been confirmed.

For now, the clearest conclusion is that Werwulf marks the end of his current run of horror-focused projects, at least for the immediate future. Eggers has not ruled out returning to monsters or supernatural stories later. He is simply expressing a desire to avoid being confined to a single genre.
seo_title: Robert Eggers Plans Horror Break After Werwulf
seo_description: Robert Eggers says he wants a break from horror after Werwulf, with a Romeo and Juliet adaptation planned as his next creative direction.
